bib.title: Effective Strategies for Asynchronous Software Engineering Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Effective Strategies for Asynchronous Software Engineering Agents" (CAID: Centralized Asynchronous Isolated Delegation), Jiayi Geng and Graham Neubig, CMU LTI. arXiv:2603.21489v2 [cs.CL], 8 Jul 2026. Preprint, 2026. Code: github.com/JiayiGeng/CAID.

COVERAGE: All 22 pages, about 86,000 chars. I read the text in full, from the abstract to the end of the appendices. I read the references only to pick up the origins. I only skimmed the later per-paper PaperBench tables (Tables 7-9 and the per-repo rows of Tables 8-9), because they repeat the Table 2 averages. The extraction was clean. I did not run the figure-caption script and took the captions from the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: CAID beats a single agent on both benchmarks and all three models, with the model held fixed.
  number: PaperBench +25.6 (MiniMax 2.5), +7.4 (GLM 4.7), +6.1 (Claude 4.5). Commit0-Lite +14.7, +3.6, +6.0.
  setup: OpenHands SDK v1.11.0. Single agent max_iterations=100. CAID has a manager at 50 iterations and engineers at 80 each, with 2 implementation rounds. PaperBench uses 2 engineers and the Code-Dev protocol with a gpt-5-mini judge. Commit0-Lite uses 4 engineers and 16 repos.
  quote: "MiniMax 2.5 reaches 36.1% under multi-agent execution, while its single-agent score is only 10.5%." / "Claude 4.5 improves from 53.1% to 59.1%, and MiniMax 2.5 reaches 57.0%"
  where: Sec 3.4, Table 2

- claim: Multi-agent costs more, and wall-clock time does not fall. Integration is sequential and test-gated.
  number: Claude on Commit0-Lite goes from 692.6 s and $1.9 (single) to 1583.2 s and $8.1 (CAID). PaperBench Claude goes from 1803.5 s and $3.3 to 2080.4 s and $6.5.
  setup: Table 2 averages.
  quote: "multi-agent execution consistently incurs higher API cost than single-agent baselines, and wall-clock runtime is not substantially reduced despite parallel execution."
  where: Sec 6, Table 2

- claim: Run a single agent first and fall back to multi-agent on failure, and you pay almost double for little gain. Start multi-agent from the outset.
  number: PaperBench Claude is 66.8 combined against 63.3 CAID. Runtime goes from 2080.4 s to 3883.9 s and cost from 6.5 to 9.7. Commit0 MiniMax stays at 57.0 for both.
  setup: Single-Agent+CAID rows in Table 2.
  quote: "the combined strategy reaches 66.8%, only slightly above the multi-agent score of 63.3%, yet runtime increases from 2080.4s to 3883.9s and cost rises from 6.5 to 9.7."
  where: Sec 3.4

- claim: Doubling the single agent's iteration budget gives little, and sometimes makes results worse.
  number: PaperBench Δ for 100 to 200 iterations is -3.0 for Claude, +1.5 for GLM and +2.8 for MiniMax (read from the Figure 2 text). Commit0 has a negative delta for MiniMax. CAID's gain over the 100-iteration baseline is 25.6 for MiniMax on PaperBench.
  setup: Single agent at max_iterations 100 against 200.
  quote: "doubling the iteration limit yields only marginal improvements and, in some cases, even degraded results."
  where: Sec 3.5, Fig 2. The extracted Figure 2 numbers are ambiguous on which delta belongs to which model or benchmark. Treat the per-model attribution as unverified.

- claim: Worktree isolation beats "soft isolation" (a shared workspace where the manager only instructs non-overlapping files). On PaperBench soft isolation is worse than a single agent.
  number: PaperBench is 57.2 single, 63.3 worktree and 55.5 soft. Commit0-Lite is 53.1 single, 59.1 worktree and 56.1 soft.
  setup: Table 3, Claude 4.5. The authors say PaperBench has no explicit file structure or dependency graph.
  quote: "on PaperBench soft isolation drops to 55.5%, below the single-agent score of 57.2%, while worktree isolation reaches 63.3%."
  where: Sec 4.1, Table 3

- claim: More engineers does not mean better results. Performance peaks, then falls once the manager cannot keep partitions disjoint.
  number: Commit0-Lite improves from 2 to 4 engineers and drops at 8. Simpy pass rate is 0.0% at N=2, 92.1% at N=4 and 44.3% at N=8. PaperBench gains little beyond 2 engineers.
  setup: Figure 3 and the Appendix D Gantt chart (Fig 6). At N=8 several engineers were given different functions in the same file (events.py), which produced overlapping writes.
  quote: "This example illustrates that scaling the number of engineers requires disciplined delegation, not simply increasing concurrency."
  where: Sec 4.2, App D

- claim: The manager's delegation choices dominate the outcome. Assigning the high-impact dependency file decides success.
  number: Minitorch pass rate is 8.7% (CAID run 1, autodiff.py never assigned), 34.3% (CAID run 2, assigned) and 17.4% (single agent).
  setup: One repo (minitorch), 3 runs, so this is anecdotal.
  quote: "Run 1 assigns engineers to several other files, but never assigns work to autodiff.py."
  where: Sec 4.3, Fig 4

- claim: More verification means more correctness and more time. Stricter manager review gives the highest pass rate and the longest runtime.
  number: Round-manager review is 60.2% at 3689.1 s. Engineer self-verification is 55.1% at 2243.9 s. Efficiency-prioritized is 54.0% at 1908.6 s.
  setup: 8 of the Commit0-Lite repos, described by the authors as a "development-stage result". The main results use self-verification.
  quote: "Round-Manager Review achieves the highest pass rate (60.2%) but also incurs the longest runtime (3689.1s)"
  where: Sec 4.4, Fig 5

- claim: The gains are statistically significant in 5 of 6 settings. Commit0 with GLM is the exception.
  number: Commit0 GLM p=0.095. PaperBench MiniMax t=5.27, p<0.0001. Commit0 Claude p=0.006.
  setup: One-sided paired t-test over 16 repos or 20 papers per model.
  quote: "GLM 4.7 improves by 3.6 points on average but does not reach significance (p= 0.095 )"
  where: App C, Table 10

- claim: Design (the mechanism, with no number attached). The manager builds a dependency graph. A unit is delegated only when all its dependencies are merged into main. Each engineer gets its own git worktree. Shared files such as __init__.py are restricted. The manager sends structured JSON assignments. The engineer self-verifies with tests before committing. A merge conflict goes back to the engineer who produced it, who pulls main, resolves it and resubmits. Main is the only source of integrated state. The manager keeps a compressed history using LLMSummarizingCondenser.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2. Primitive mapping in Table 1.
  quote: "If a merge conflict occurs, the engineer who produced the conflicting commit is responsible for resolving it."
  where: Sec 2.1-2.5

LIMITS
- Authors concede the cost and runtime overhead and no wall-clock speedup.
- Delegation is prompt heuristics, not a learned policy.
- The evaluation is SWE-only. Other domains would need new isolation and validation mechanisms.
- It is a single framework (OpenHands) with 3 models and a small iteration budget. Commit0-Lite is 16 repos. PaperBench uses Code-Dev only, with a gpt-5-mini judge, not the full pipeline.
- Single runs, with no reported variance except the t-tests. The Figure 4 comparison is a single repo.
- Some gains are weak. GLM on Commit0 is not significant, and CAID regresses on some repos (for example tinydb by -10.5 for GLM).
- Per-repo tables show CAID falling below the single agent in several cases.

BUILDS ON
- Cemri et al. 2025 (why multi-agent systems fail; free-form dialog misalignment as the primary failure mode).
- Khatua et al. 2026 (CooperBench; concurrent edits and merge conflicts).
- Cognition AI 2025 ("Don't build multi-agents"; late discovery of conflicts).
- Zhao et al. 2024 (Commit0). Starace et al. 2025 (PaperBench). Wang et al. 2024 and 2025a (OpenHands and the SDK).
- Hong et al. 2023 (MetaGPT). Qian et al. 2024a (ChatDev). Qian et al. 2024b and Li et al. 2024a (scaling the number of agents). Yang et al. 2026 (agent scaling and diversity).
- Radar 2024 (O'Reilly) and Bhavsar 2026 (Galileo blog) are cited for coordination overhead and handoff failure.

CODE: There is no code. The appendix has the manager prompts (A.1 for Commit0, A.2 for PaperBench). The delegation JSON schema is the reusable piece.
- Task shape: "assign_task": {"reasoning", "assignments":[{"engineer_id","task_id","file_path","functions_to_implement","instruction","complexity":"simple|medium|complex"}]}
- Round-1 shape: "delegation_plan": {"first_round":{"num_agents","reasoning","tasks":[...]}, "remaining_tasks":[{"task_id","file_path","functions_to_implement","complexity","depends_on":[...]}]}
- Readiness rule (Sec 2.1): Ready_t(v_j) ⇔ ∀(v_i,v_j)∈E, v_i∈C_t.
- Prompt instructions worth keeping: "Keep highly interdependent files within the same major task." "If two files are circularly dependent, assign them to the same engineer." "Do NOT assign multiple engineers to modify the same file, as this will cause merge conflicts." "Do NOT provide any code snippets or pseudo-code." The manager does not write the implementation.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): CAID workflow. It shows the manager, the engineers in worktrees, merge to main, and reassignment. It is the quickest overview of the architecture.
- Table 1 (p2): maps SWE primitives to coordination mechanisms.
- Fig 2: gain from CAID against gain from extra iterations.
- Table 3: worktree against soft isolation.
- Fig 3: engineer count against runtime, score and cost.
- Fig 4: minitorch Gantt charts showing how delegation drives the outcome.
- Fig 5: verification intensity against runtime.
- Fig 6 (App D): simpy at N=2, 4 and 8, showing the file-level overlap failure.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. The extraction of Table 2, Figure 2 and the per-repo tables is column-jumbled (for example "63.36.8..." where the values are 63.3 and 66.8). I took the numbers I quote from the prose and table rows, and they agree with each other. The Figure 2 per-model delta attribution is ambiguous. I skimmed Tables 7-9 (the PaperBench tables for GLM and MiniMax). The target note 07-orchestration.md already exists. Its header cites other sources and does not cite this paper, and I did not compare the two in detail.
